data.title: Ritual Bowl
data.summary: A wide, speckled stoneware bowl for breakfast grains, soups and slow afternoon fruit.

image.alt: Speckled oatmeal stoneware bowl on a pale background
Large speckled bowl on a linen-covered table beside a smaller green bowl

images.caption: At home on the table with the Moss Serving Bowl.

data.material: Wheel-thrown stoneware with natural iron speckle, finished in a satin oatmeal glaze. The foot ring is left unglazed to show the raw clay.
data.care: Dishwasher safe on a gentle cycle; hand washing keeps the satin finish longest. Microwave safe. Avoid sudden temperature changes, such as moving from the fridge to a hot oven.

children.text: The Ritual Bowl began as a test piece for the studio's breakfast table and stayed because nobody wanted to give theirs back.
Each one is thrown, trimmed and glazed by hand, so the speckle pattern and the line where the glaze breaks over the rim are never quite the same twice.

data.title: Grounded Mug
data.summary: A straight-sided mug with a generous handle, sized for a proper morning pour.

image.alt: Warm brown stoneware mug with a rounded handle

images.caption: Toasted clay body with a thin clear liner.

data.material: Toasted stoneware clay, glazed clear on the inside and left with a soft matte skin outside. Holds about 320 ml.
data.care: Dishwasher and microwave safe. The matte exterior can pick up marks from metal cutlery; a little baking soda on a damp cloth lifts them.

children.text: We pulled the handle wider than usual so it sits comfortably for two fingers and a thumb, even with gloves on during winter markets.

data.title: Solace Vase
data.summary: A small, softly lopsided bud vase pinched by hand from a single ball of clay.

image.alt: Rounded brown bud vase with a narrow neck

images.caption: Every Solace Vase leans its own way.

data.material: Hand-pinched stoneware in an unglazed toasted finish, with a sealed interior so it holds water.
data.care: Hand wash only. Empty and dry between uses; the unglazed exterior darkens slightly where it gets wet and returns to its colour as it dries.

children.text: The Solace Vase is made without the wheel. Its shape comes from the pressure of two thumbs and a lot of patience, which is why no two lean the same way.
It is available by inquiry only while we build up a small batch.

data.title: Moss Serving Bowl
data.summary: A deep serving bowl in a mottled green glaze that pools darker in the curve.

image.alt: Green glazed stoneware bowl on a linen tablecloth
Still life of stoneware bowls and a handled vase with olive branches on a linen table

images.caption: Shown with the Ritual Bowl and Hollow Handle Vessel.

data.material: Stoneware with a moss-green ash glaze. The glaze varies from sage to deep olive depending on its place in the kiln.
data.care: Dishwasher safe. Suitable for serving warm food; not for use on a stovetop or under a grill.

children.text: The moss glaze is mixed in the studio from a recipe we adjust with every new bag of ash, so each firing lands in a slightly different green.

data.title: Shallow Dish
data.summary: A low dish for rings, keys, salt or a single candle.

images.caption: Trimmed from the same clay as the Ritual Bowl.

data.material: Speckled stoneware in the satin oatmeal glaze, with an unglazed base.
data.care: Wipe clean or hand wash. Safe for tea lights; place on a heat-resistant surface.

children.text: Shallow Dishes are made from the clay left over at the end of a throwing day, which keeps the studio's waste low and the dishes small and varied.

data.title: Hollow Handle Vessel
data.summary: A tall, hand-built vessel with a pierced handle and a two-tone dipped base.

image.alt: Tall speckled stoneware vessel with a pierced handle holding olive branches
Olive sprig resting on a folded linen cloth

data.material: Coil-built stoneware. The upper body is left raw, the lower third is dipped in a darker slip for a quiet two-tone line.
data.care: Hand wash only. Watertight for fresh stems; change the water every few days.

children.text: This is the slowest piece we make. It is coiled over three days, left to firm up, and then pierced while the clay is leather-hard.
We make a handful each season. If the shop shows none in stock, send us an inquiry and we will tell you when the next firing is due.
Ines set up the studio in a former bakery after years of throwing at a shared community kiln. She makes most of the tableware and every Solace Vase.
She cares about pieces that are used daily rather than kept for best, and tests every new form at her own table for a month before it joins the collection.
Theo looks after the glaze shelf and the kiln schedule. The moss glaze and the dipped two-tone line on the Hollow Handle Vessel both started as his experiments.
He keeps a notebook of every firing, which is why we can tell you roughly when the next batch of a piece will be ready.

data.title: Our story
data.lede: A two-person ceramics studio making objects for everyday rituals: the first coffee, a shared meal, a branch brought in from a walk.

image.alt: Folded linen cloth on a table with an olive sprig

children.text: Atelier is a small, invented studio created to show how a maker can present a focused collection. Everything here is thrown, pinched or coiled by hand, then fired in small batches.
We would rather make fewer pieces well than fill a warehouse. That is why some pieces are sold through partner shops, and others are made to order after a short conversation.

Clay is wedged and thrown in the morning, trimmed the next day and left to dry slowly under cloth. Glazes are mixed in the studio. A typical piece takes three to four weeks from wet clay to the shelf.

data.title: Contact
data.lede: Questions about a piece, a custom set or a visit to the studio? Send us a note and we will reply within a few working days.

children.text: We do not take payments on this site. When a piece is available, we will point you to the partner shop that stocks it or arrange the details with you directly.
